benchmark_kind: single-host A/B crossover measurement on a controlled synthetic fixture
protocol: MP-SPDZ Semi, three local parties, preprocessing included
scope_warning: Synthetic fixture on a single host, one query. It demonstrates the layout crossover under controlled degree skew; it is not a MetaQA, WebQSP, WAN, or production result, and all three parties ran on one machine, which does not instantiate the non-collusion assumption.
headline_finding: On a fixture with source-degree skew, the relation-paged backend is 23.6x faster and uses 17.5x less communication than the packed scan, at identical semantics and identical results. Together with benchmarks/relation_paged_backend_ab.json, which shows the paged backend 1.15x SLOWER on a fixture with no skew, this locates the crossover: the paged layout wins in proportion to how much wider the maximum source degree is than the maximum (source, relation) degree.

fixture.note: Both configurations describe exactly the same edges, so this measures layout cost at identical semantics.

predicted_advantage_from_cost_model.note: Measured 17.5x communication sits between the 12.1x product ratio and the 52.8x unpack ratio, consistent with cost being split between linear-scan products and bit-decomposition of packed records.

correctness.comparison: Exact JSON equality of all four reconstructed ranked rows, across two backends and two independently implemented cleartext oracles.

what_this_does_not_show: Any real-dataset result; the degree skew here is synthetic and controlled.
Overflow-page behaviour: pages_per_key is 1 in this fixture; the multi-page path is validated separately in relation_paged_overflow_validation.json.
Any malicious-security property; MP-SPDZ Semi is passive-only.
That the paged layout is always preferable: on an unskewed fixture it is measurably slower.
